title: The error told you to delete one line. Deleting it changed every answer.
summary:
A breaking change that fails loudly, and a fix that changes your product silently.

The error told you to delete one line. Deleting it changed every answer your product gives.

What changed

Anthropic's API version 2026-10-21 removed temperature, top_p and top_k from the Messages API. Not deprecated with a grace period. Removed.

The migration guide states it plainly:

In 2026-10-21, a request that sends temperature, top_p, or top_k returns a 400 error, even at the parameter's default value.

So this is a loud failure. Your request breaks, the error names the parameter, and you know exactly what to do.

That part is fine. Loud failures get fixed.

The part that is not loud

The fix is to delete the parameter. The guide then tells you what happens next:

Without these parameters, a request samples with their defaults, including a temperature of 1.0, the same as a 2023-06-01 request that leaves them out.

Your line said 0.0. You deleted it. You are now sampling at 1.0.

And for the models where that difference was real:

On models that accept other values, such as Claude Sonnet 4.6, a request that lowered temperature for more consistent output loses that effect. No other setting replaces it.

No other setting replaces it. That sentence is the whole article.

The sequence, as it actually plays out 

# Before: 2023-06-01, pinned low for a structured extraction task
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    temperature=0.0,          # <- deliberate. consistency matters here.
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
)

You bump the SDK. The call fails with a 400 — something to this effect (exact wording illustrative; the documented behaviour is a 400):

anthropic.BadRequestError: 400 - temperature is not supported
in API version 2026-10-21

You do the obvious thing:

# After: the 400 is gone
resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
)

Green. Tests pass. Ship it.

What actually happened:

  1. You upgraded. A 400 appeared. The error named the parameter.
  2. You deleted the parameter. The 400 went away.
  3. Your tests passed — because your tests assert on shape, not on distribution.
  4. Your product's output variance is permanently higher, and nothing in your pipeline said so.

Step 2 is where it happens. The fix that silences an error is not the fix that preserves behaviour. And an error message is written to be silenced — that is its entire job.

Why your test suite will not catch this

Most LLM test suites look like this:

def test_extraction():
    out = extract(SAMPLE_INVOICE)
    assert out["invoice_no"] == "INV-2291"
    assert isinstance(out["line_items"], list)
    assert out["total"] == 118000

That is a shape and value assertion on one sample. At temperature=0.0 it was close to a deterministic check. At 1.0 it is a sample from a distribution that now happens to pass.

It will keep passing. Right up until the day it does not, on a customer's document, in production, with no code change to blame.

What catches it instead:

def test_extraction_is_stable():
    runs = [extract(SAMPLE_INVOICE) for _ in range(20)]
    distinct = {json.dumps(r, sort_keys=True) for r in runs}
    # not "did it work once" but "does it work the same way"
    assert len(distinct) == 1, f"{len(distinct)} distinct outputs in 20 runs"

Slower. More expensive. The only thing that would have told you.

To be fair to the guide

The escape hatch is documented:

If a request relies on a non-default value, either stop sending the parameter, or keep that request on 2023-06-01.

It is right there. It sits in the paragraph most people stop reading after sentence one, immediately below the instruction that fixes their build.

That is not a documentation failure. It is a reading failure, and it is extremely common: when an error message and a fix appear in the same paragraph, the rest of the paragraph does not get read.

The discipline

When a breaking change hands you a fix, ask what the fix changes. "Remove it" is a behaviour change wearing an error message.

Treat sampling settings as product config, not tuning knobs. Write down which of your outputs depend on low variance — structured extraction, classification, anything feeding a downstream parser — and which genuinely do not.

Test distribution, not shape. Run one prompt 20 times and diff them. A schema check will never catch this.

Record the API version your behaviour was measured against, beside the measurement. An eval result without its API version is an incomplete artefact.

Two hard rules

An error you silenced is not a bug you fixed.

If removing a setting is the official fix, that setting was doing something.

While you are in there

From the same source, one dated item worth putting in a calendar:

Deprecated model Retires Recommended replacement
claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 30 November 2026 claude-sonnet-5-5

And the lifecycle definition, verbatim: "Retired: The model is no longer available for use. Requests to retired models fail."

That one, at least, is not silent.

Anthropic also states it provides "at least 60 days' notice before model retirement for publicly released models" — and the console has a usage export that breaks your traffic down by API key and model, which is the fastest way to find out whether a deprecated model is still in your path.

Honest limitation

I am reading Anthropic's own migration guide and model-deprecation page, and every quote above comes from them.

I have not measured the variance change on a production workload. How large it is depends entirely on your prompts: a tightly constrained extraction prompt with a rigid schema may move barely at all, while an open-ended generation task may move a lot. The point is not the size of the effect. The point is that the change happened and nothing told you.

Checkable references

  • "Migrating to API version 2026-10-21" — Claude platform docs
  • "Model deprecations" — Claude platform docs

One open question

When you removed temperature to clear that 400 — did anyone measure the output before and after?

title: Price comparison: Amazon, AliExpress, eBay, Walmart, Etsy with Python
summary:
What does a ceramic mug cost online? It depends where you look: Amazon, AliExpress, eBay, Walmart and Etsy each show different products, different sellers, different shipping terms and very different prices for the same words. Sellers who source or price a product, and anyone building a price comparison page, need those five answers side by side, in the same columns. This tutorial does a price comparison across Amazon, AliExpress, eBay, Walmart and Etsy with Python: one keyword, one run, one table, then the cheapest product on each marketplace and a price summary per marketplace with pandas. The data comes from the Marketplace Price Comparison Actor on Apify, called through the official Python client.

What you need

  • An Apify account (the free plan is enough to try this) and its API token, from Apify Console → Settings → API & Integrations, exported as an environment variable: export APIFY_TOKEN=...
  • Python 3 and two packages: 
pip install "apify-client>=3,<4" pandas

The common table

The Actor searches every marketplace for the same keywords in one run and returns one flat row per product, with the same columns whatever the marketplace:

  • marketplace (amazon, aliexpress, ebay, walmart or etsy), searchQuery and rankInMarketplace, the product's position in that marketplace's best-match order;
  • title, url, imageUrl, platformProductId (the marketplace's own id) and, when shown, brand and category;
  • price and currency, originalPrice and discountPercent for a deal, inStock;
  • shippingFree, shippingCost, deliveryEstimate, shipsFrom;
  • rating on 5, reviewCount, soldCount (units sold, where the marketplace publishes it), storeType (platform, business, individual or unknown) and isSponsored.

A value a marketplace does not show is null, so a CSV export keeps the same columns from run to run. Private sellers are never named; review texts and their authors are never collected.

Step 1: the input 

run_input = {
    "searchQueries": ["ceramic mug"],
    "marketplaces": ["amazon", "aliexpress", "ebay", "walmart", "etsy"],
    "maxResultsPerMarketplace": 20,
    "country": "US",
}

This is the public task "Compare ceramic mug prices on Etsy, eBay and AliExpress", with Amazon and Walmart added. country picks each marketplace's site (amazon.com, ebay.com, walmart.com, etsy.com, AliExpress shipping to the US) and the currency, USD here. maxResultsPerMarketplace caps the products per keyword and marketplace, so this run returns at most 100 rows.

Choose the keyword with Etsy in mind: Etsy only has results for common product words such as "ceramic mug" or "phone case". For "wireless earbuds" or "air fryer", keep the default marketplaces (Amazon, AliExpress, eBay and Walmart). Other useful fields: condition (new or used), and priceMin / priceMax for a price range, applied by each marketplace's filter and checked again on every product.

Step 2: run it and save the table

Save this as compare_prices.py:

import os

import pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

run_input = {
    "searchQueries": ["ceramic mug"],
    "marketplaces": ["amazon", "aliexpress", "ebay", "walmart", "etsy"],
    "maxResultsPerMarketplace": 20,
    "country": "US",
}

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("myth84/marketplace-price-compare-scraper").call(run_input=run_input)
rows = list(client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).iterate_items())

for item in rows[:8]:
    print(item["marketplace"], item["rankInMarketplace"], item["price"], item["currency"], item["title"][:60])

df = pd.json_normalize(rows)
columns = [
    "marketplace", "rankInMarketplace", "title", "price", "currency", "shippingFree", "shippingCost",
    "deliveryEstimate", "rating", "reviewCount", "soldCount", "storeType", "isSponsored", "url",
]
df[columns].to_csv("ceramic-mug-5-marketplaces.csv", index=False)
print(df["marketplace"].value_counts())

pd.json_normalize turns each row into one line and flattens attributes, the small object of facts that only some marketplaces show, into columns such as attributes.condition (eBay and Walmart) or attributes.boughtPastMonth (Amazon's "bought in past month", a monthly lower bound). The CSV is the common table: one line per product, whatever the marketplace.

Step 3: the cheapest on each marketplace

Three things to know before calling a product "the cheapest":

  • Welcome deals. AliExpress shows part of its products at a price for first-time buyers only, flagged by attributes.newShopperDeal. That price is not one anybody can pay, so leave those rows out.
  • No featured offer. Amazon shows some products without a price, when no seller has the featured offer: price is empty, and the filter below leaves those rows out.
  • Shipping. price is the displayed price, shipping not included. shippingCost gives the shipping price when the marketplace shows it; shippingFree is true when shipping is free and empty when the marketplace says nothing.

Add this to the script:

welcome = df.get("attributes.newShopperDeal", pd.Series("false", index=df.index)).eq("true")
anyone = df[~welcome & df["price"].notna() & (df["currency"] == "USD")].copy()
anyone["withShipping"] = anyone["price"] + anyone["shippingCost"].fillna(0)

cheapest = anyone.sort_values("withShipping").groupby("marketplace").head(1)
print(cheapest[["marketplace", "title", "price", "shippingCost", "withShipping", "url"]].to_string(index=False))

summary = anyone.groupby("marketplace").agg(
    products=("title", "count"),
    lowest=("price", "min"),
    median=("price", "median"),
    highest=("price", "max"),
    medianRating=("rating", "median"),
    medianSold=("soldCount", "median"),
)
print(summary.sort_values("median"))

cheapest holds one line per marketplace: the lowest price shipping included, as far as each marketplace shows it, with the link. summary gives, per marketplace, the number of products compared, the lowest, median and highest price, the median rating and the median units sold (empty where the marketplace publishes no sales figure, such as Amazon and Walmart). The median is the number to look at: one very cheap accessory or one premium set can make the lowest and highest misleading, and the median says what the typical product of the first results costs.

The comparison stays within one currency: no exchange rate is applied, which is why the filter keeps the US dollar rows. For the full rows of a marketplace, filter the DataFrame on marketplace and sort it by soldCount or rating.

Several keywords, every day

searchQueries takes several lines; each keyword is compared separately, and searchQuery tells the rows apart. Group by ["searchQuery", "marketplace"] instead of "marketplace" and the summary covers your whole catalogue in one run.

To follow a market over time, run the script every morning with cron and append the summary to a CSV with today's date: the median price of each marketplace, day after day, shows who moves first. Without code, open the public task in Apify Console, change the keyword, save it as your own task and add a daily schedule; the Output tab has a Comparison view of the products and a summary record per keyword and marketplace with the lowest, median and highest price.

Good to know

  • Each marketplace's own best-match order, sponsored products included and flagged in isSponsored; rankInMarketplace is the position among the rows of the run.
  • One marketplace failing does not stop the others: its status and the reason are in the run log and the summary record. The run fails only when no marketplace returned anything.
  • Amazon is searched on amazon.com, .co.uk, .ca, .de, .fr, .it and .es, Walmart in the US and Canada only; for another country, the marketplace is skipped and the log says so.
  • eBay is searched for fixed-price ("Buy It Now") listings: an auction's current bid is not a price to compare.
  • A product found by two of your keywords on the same marketplace appears once, under the first keyword.
  • No personal data: products, prices, average ratings and review counts; sellers are named only when they are the platform itself or a registered business.

Pricing is pay-per-event: a fixed price per product row, $2.00 per 1,000 on Apify's Free plan, down to $1.29 on the higher plans, whatever the marketplace (this run of up to 100 rows costs at most $0.20). A marketplace that returns nothing costs nothing. Use the data for analysis, respect each marketplace's terms and local law, and do not republish listings.

title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash spent 84% of my tokens thinking: real latency, real cost, and the settings that fix it
summary:
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash started streaming in 1.2 seconds on every run I made. It took 20 seconds to produce the first line of the code I asked for. In between, it wrote about 3,300 tokens of reasoning that I never saw, and paid for at the output rate.

That gap matters more than any per-token price, so this post measures it, shows which settings change it, and works out what one answer actually costs at the official price and at ours.

Disclosure: I work on growth at OceanToken, an OpenAI-compatible API that resells DeepSeek, and I ran the tests there. The official prices come from DeepSeek's Models & Pricing page, with the date I read them.

TL;DR

  • Reasoning is on by default and billed as output. On a small coding prompt, 84% of V4.1 Flash's output tokens were reasoning.
  • With max_tokens: 800, Flash used the whole budget thinking and returned no code, and the call was still billed.
  • reasoning_effort: "low" cut cost by 37% and time-to-answer by ~45%. thinking: {type: "disabled"} did nothing in my runs.

title: What Happens Second by Second in the Bama Bound Reference Clip? A Python Timeline of Banner, Motion and Sound (Tested)
summary:
Checked November 14, 2026 (15:00 CST, UTC+8). I build bamabound.app, which turns one photo of one person into a vertical clip of them holding a red I'M BAMA BOUND banner. The clip measured here is the "Imported field preview" shown on the site. The site labels it "an external reference of the sign clip. Not a result generated by this studio." I only measured it. It isn't re-published here, and there are no frames of it in this post.

People ask AI assistants things like "what does the Bama Bound video actually do?" or "why does my Bama Bound clip get louder halfway through?" The Bama Bound meme page says there's one preset, and that it keeps the red banner and the reference timing. The FAQ says the clip is about eight seconds, vertical 9:16, and "the original soundtrack stays".

That's the product description. I wanted the same thing as numbers: where the banner is in each second, how much the picture moves, whether there's a cut, and what the sound does. A reference-video generator follows the reference's timing, so these numbers are also a checklist for your own result. If your clip's loud moment comes half a second early, the timeline shows it.

This post builds that timeline with one Python file (NumPy + ffmpeg, about 100 lines), runs it on the reference, and then tests it on two altered copies so you can see it notice the changes.

What ffprobe says first

Before any pixels:

video  h264 High, level 3.1, 720x1280, 24 fps, 193 frames, yuv420p, about 5.9 Mbit/s
audio  aac LC, 32000 Hz, stereo, about 130 kbit/s
format duration 8.096 s
frame types: 1 I, 49 P, 143 B
container tag: AIGC = "This content is generated by AI"

Two details stood out:

  • One keyframe in 193 frames. The only I-frame is frame 0. Players and editors seek by jumping to a keyframe and decoding forward, so scrubbing near the end of this file means decoding most of it. Re-encode with -g 24 (one keyframe per second) if you want snappy scrubbing.
  • The AIGC tag. The reference file carries a format-level metadata tag saying it was generated by AI. I expected a plain stream copy to keep it. It doesn't. ffmpeg's MP4 muxer only writes standard keys unless you ask for custom ones: 
$ ffprobe -v error -show_entries format_tags=AIGC -of default=nw=1 
source:            TAG:AIGC={This content is generated by AI}
-c copy -> (no tag)
-c copy -map_metadata -1 -> (no tag)
re-encode (libx264) -> (no tag)
-c copy -movflags +use_metadata_tags -> TAG:AIGC={This content is generated by AI}
re-encode -movflags +use_metadata_tags -> TAG:AIGC={This content is generated by AI}

So every ordinary edit, even a lossless trim with -c copy, silently drops the AI label. Add -movflags +use_metadata_tags if you want it kept (and label the post on the platform too; I haven't checked which apps read this tag).

The script

timeline.py decodes the clip at 180x320 (small enough that grain averages out, big enough to find the banner), and computes three things per frame:

  • banner area: the share of pixels that look like the banner's crimson (r > 1.6·g, r > 1.2·b, r − g > 25). On the reference, the banner cloth measures around RGB (77, 34, 52), dark crimson rather than bright red, which is why the thresholds are ratios and not "r > 200".
  • banner top: the first row (as a fraction of frame height) where at least 25% of the row is banner-coloured. That row-coverage rule stops a few reddish skin pixels from counting as the banner.
  • motion: the mean absolute grey-level change against the previous frame, 0-255.

For sound it mixes to mono at the file's own sample rate and takes RMS in dBFS per half-second. It also looks for the biggest "step up" in loudness: 0.1 s RMS blocks, the median of the next 0.5 s minus the median of the previous 0.5 s. A frame counts as a cut when its motion is over 6x the clip's median and over 12.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Per-second timeline of a short vertical clip: banner position, motion, cuts, sound.

usage: python3 timeline.py clip.mp4 [--csv frames.csv]
Needs ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH and NumPy. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Per frame (decoded at 180x320):
  banner_area  share of pixels that look like the crimson banner (r > 1.6*g, r > 1.2*b, r-g > 25)
  banner_top   first row (0..1 of frame height) where >= 25% of a row is banner-coloured
  motion       mean absolute grey-level change vs the previous frame (0..255)
Per 0.5 s of audio (mono mix at the file's own sample rate): RMS in dBFS,
plus the biggest 'step up' in loudness (0.1 s RMS, median 0.5 s after minus before).
A "cut" is a frame whose motion is > 6x the median motion and > 12.
"""
import json, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np

W, H = 180, 320

def probe(path):
    out = subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-show_entries",
        "stream=codec_type,width,height,r_frame_rate,sample_rate,channels:format=duration",
        "-of", "json", path], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
    return json.loads(out)

def frames(path):
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-vf", f"scale={W}:{H}",
        "-f", "rawvideo", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-"], capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.uint8).reshape(-1, H, W, 3)

def audio(path, rate):
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-vn", "-ac", "1", "-ar", str(rate),
        "-f", "f32le", "-"], capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32)

def main():
    path = sys.argv[1]
    csv = sys.argv[sys.argv.index("--csv") + 1] if "--csv" in sys.argv else None
    info = probe(path)
    v = next(s for s in info["streams"] if s["codec_type"] == "video")
    a = next((s for s in info["streams"] if s["codec_type"] == "audio"), None)
    num, den = map(int, v["r_frame_rate"].split("/")); fps = num / den
    f = frames(path).astype(np.int16)
    r, g, b = f[..., 0], f[..., 1], f[..., 2]
    mask = (r * 10 > g * 16) & (r * 10 > b * 12) & (r - g > 25)
    area = mask.mean(axis=(1, 2))
    rows = mask.mean(axis=2) >= 0.25
    top = np.array([np.argmax(x) / H if x.any() else np.nan for x in rows])
    grey = f.mean(axis=3)
    motion = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.abs(np.diff(grey, axis=0)).mean(axis=(1, 2))])
    med = float(np.median(motion[1:]))
    cuts = [i for i in range(1, len(motion)) if motion[i] > 6 * med and motion[i] > 12]
    print(f"file      {path}")
    print(f"video     {v['width']}x{v['height']} @ {fps:g} fps, {len(f)} frames, "
          f"container duration {float(info['format']['duration']):.3f} s")
    if a:
        print(f"audio     {a['sample_rate']} Hz, {a['channels']} ch")
    print(f"motion    median {med:.2f}, max {motion.max():.2f} at frame {int(motion.argmax())} "
          f"({motion.argmax() / fps:.2f} s)")
    print(f"cuts      {len(cuts)}" + (": " + ", ".join(f'{c / fps:.2f}s' for c in cuts) if cuts else ""))
    print(f"banner    visible (area >= 3%) in {int((area >= 0.03).sum())}/{len(f)} frames; "
          f"area {area.min():.3f}-{area.max():.3f}; top edge {np.nanmin(top):.3f}-{np.nanmax(top):.3f} of height")
    snd = None
    if a:
        rate = int(a['sample_rate']); x = audio(path, rate); hop = rate // 2
        snd = [20 * np.log10(np.sqrt(np.mean(x[i:i + hop] ** 2)) + 1e-9) for i in range(0, len(x) - hop + 1, hop)]
        h10 = rate // 10
        fine = np.array([20 * np.log10(np.sqrt(np.mean(x[i:i + h10] ** 2)) + 1e-9)
                         for i in range(0, len(x) - h10 + 1, h10)])
        rise = [(np.median(fine[k:k + 5]) - np.median(fine[k - 5:k]), k / 10) for k in range(5, len(fine) - 4)]
        db, t = max(rise)
        print(f"sound     biggest step up: {db:+.1f} dB at {t:.1f} s (median of 0.5 s after vs before)")
    print("\n  second | banner area | banner top | motion | sound dBFS (two halves)")
    for s in range(int(np.ceil(len(f) / fps))):
        sl = slice(int(round(s * fps)), int(round((s + 1) * fps)))
        if sl.start >= len(f):
            break
        snd_txt = ""
        if snd:
            pair = snd[2 * s:2 * s + 2]
            snd_txt = " / ".join(f"{d:6.1f}" for d in pair)
        print(f"  {s:>2}-{s + 1:<3} |    {area[sl].mean():.3f}    |   {np.nanmean(top[sl]):.3f}    | {motion[sl].mean():6.2f} | {snd_txt}")
    if csv:
        with open(csv, "w") as fh:
            fh.write("frame,t,banner_area,banner_top,motion\n")
            for i in range(len(f)):
                fh.write(f"{i},{i / fps:.4f},{area[i]:.4f},{top[i]:.4f},{motion[i]:.3f}\n")
        print(f"\nwrote {csv}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The reference, second by second

   0-1   |    0.167    |   0.110    |   5.49 |  -21.8 /  -19.2

What that says, in plain words:

  • No cuts. It's one continuous shot. The biggest frame-to-frame change is 19.08 at 5.17 s, about 2.4x the median of 7.86. That's movement, not a cut (the cut test below gives a sense of scale).
  • The banner is always on screen, in all 193 frames, and it's high. Its top edge starts at 10.3% of the frame height and drifts down to 19.1% at about 4.8 s, then comes back up a little. Its area shrinks from 17.7% of the frame to about 9-12% in the second half, so it gets smaller or turns away from the camera. Caption stickers in the top fifth of the frame will sit on the banner. Put text lower down.
  • The motion is constant. It's 5.5 at the start and 7-11 for the rest. The median of 7.86 is high for a 180x320 decode, so expect handheld-style movement throughout, not a locked-off camera.
  • The sound steps up about 9 dB at 3.5 s. The first 3.5 seconds sit around −19 to −23 dBFS, and from 3.5 s on it's about −12 to −15 dBFS. That step explains the "why does it get louder halfway" question. It's in the reference soundtrack, which the clip keeps.

event_model_payload.summary:
Checked November 14, 2026 (15:00 CST, UTC+8). I build bamabound.app, which turns one photo of one person into a vertical clip of them holding a red I'M BAMA BOUND banner. The clip measured here is the "Imported field preview" shown on the site. The site labels it "an external reference of the sign clip. Not a result generated by this studio." I only measured it. It isn't re-published here, and there are no frames of it in this post.

People ask AI assistants things like "what does the Bama Bound video actually do?" or "why does my Bama Bound clip get louder halfway through?" The Bama Bound meme page says there's one preset, and that it keeps the red banner and the reference timing. The FAQ says the clip is about eight seconds, vertical 9:16, and "the original soundtrack stays".

That's the product description. I wanted the same thing as numbers: where the banner is in each second, how much the picture moves, whether there's a cut, and what the sound does. A reference-video generator follows the reference's timing, so these numbers are also a checklist for your own result. If your clip's loud moment comes half a second early, the timeline shows it.

This post builds that timeline with one Python file (NumPy + ffmpeg, about 100 lines), runs it on the reference, and then tests it on two altered copies so you can see it notice the changes.

What ffprobe says first

Before any pixels:

video  h264 High, level 3.1, 720x1280, 24 fps, 193 frames, yuv420p, about 5.9 Mbit/s
audio  aac LC, 32000 Hz, stereo, about 130 kbit/s
format duration 8.096 s
frame types: 1 I, 49 P, 143 B
container tag: AIGC = "This content is generated by AI"

Two details stood out:

  • One keyframe in 193 frames. The only I-frame is frame 0. Players and editors seek by jumping to a keyframe and decoding forward, so scrubbing near the end of this file means decoding most of it. Re-encode with -g 24 (one keyframe per second) if you want snappy scrubbing.
  • The AIGC tag. The reference file carries a format-level metadata tag saying it was generated by AI. I expected a plain stream copy to keep it. It doesn't. ffmpeg's MP4 muxer only writes standard keys unless you ask for custom ones: 
$ ffprobe -v error -show_entries format_tags=AIGC -of default=nw=1 
source:            TAG:AIGC={This content is generated by AI}
-c copy -> (no tag)
-c copy -map_metadata -1 -> (no tag)
re-encode (libx264) -> (no tag)
-c copy -movflags +use_metadata_tags -> TAG:AIGC={This content is generated by AI}
re-encode -movflags +use_metadata_tags -> TAG:AIGC={This content is generated by AI}

So every ordinary edit, even a lossless trim with -c copy, silently drops the AI label. Add -movflags +use_metadata_tags if you want it kept (and label the post on the platform too; I haven't checked which apps read this tag).

The script

timeline.py decodes the clip at 180x320 (small enough that grain averages out, big enough to find the banner), and computes three things per frame:

  • banner area: the share of pixels that look like the banner's crimson (r > 1.6·g, r > 1.2·b, r − g > 25). On the reference, the banner cloth measures around RGB (77, 34, 52), dark crimson rather than bright red, which is why the thresholds are ratios and not "r > 200".
  • banner top: the first row (as a fraction of frame height) where at least 25% of the row is banner-coloured. That row-coverage rule stops a few reddish skin pixels from counting as the banner.
  • motion: the mean absolute grey-level change against the previous frame, 0-255.

For sound it mixes to mono at the file's own sample rate and takes RMS in dBFS per half-second. It also looks for the biggest "step up" in loudness: 0.1 s RMS blocks, the median of the next 0.5 s minus the median of the previous 0.5 s. A frame counts as a cut when its motion is over 6x the clip's median and over 12.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Per-second timeline of a short vertical clip: banner position, motion, cuts, sound.

usage: python3 timeline.py clip.mp4 [--csv frames.csv]
Needs ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH and NumPy. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Per frame (decoded at 180x320):
  banner_area  share of pixels that look like the crimson banner (r > 1.6*g, r > 1.2*b, r-g > 25)
  banner_top   first row (0..1 of frame height) where >= 25% of a row is banner-coloured
  motion       mean absolute grey-level change vs the previous frame (0..255)
Per 0.5 s of audio (mono mix at the file's own sample rate): RMS in dBFS,
plus the biggest 'step up' in loudness (0.1 s RMS, median 0.5 s after minus before).
A "cut" is a frame whose motion is > 6x the median motion and > 12.
"""
import json, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np

W, H = 180, 320

def probe(path):
    out = subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-show_entries",
        "stream=codec_type,width,height,r_frame_rate,sample_rate,channels:format=duration",
        "-of", "json", path], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
    return json.loads(out)

def frames(path):
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-vf", f"scale={W}:{H}",
        "-f", "rawvideo", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-"], capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.uint8).reshape(-1, H, W, 3)

def audio(path, rate):
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-vn", "-ac", "1", "-ar", str(rate),
        "-f", "f32le", "-"], capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32)

def main():
    path = sys.argv[1]
    csv = sys.argv[sys.argv.index("--csv") + 1] if "--csv" in sys.argv else None
    info = probe(path)
    v = next(s for s in info["streams"] if s["codec_type"] == "video")
    a = next((s for s in info["streams"] if s["codec_type"] == "audio"), None)
    num, den = map(int, v["r_frame_rate"].split("/")); fps = num / den
    f = frames(path).astype(np.int16)
    r, g, b = f[..., 0], f[..., 1], f[..., 2]
    mask = (r * 10 > g * 16) & (r * 10 > b * 12) & (r - g > 25)
    area = mask.mean(axis=(1, 2))
    rows = mask.mean(axis=2) >= 0.25
    top = np.array([np.argmax(x) / H if x.any() else np.nan for x in rows])
    grey = f.mean(axis=3)
    motion = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.abs(np.diff(grey, axis=0)).mean(axis=(1, 2))])
    med = float(np.median(motion[1:]))
    cuts = [i for i in range(1, len(motion)) if motion[i] > 6 * med and motion[i] > 12]
    print(f"file      {path}")
    print(f"video     {v['width']}x{v['height']} @ {fps:g} fps, {len(f)} frames, "
          f"container duration {float(info['format']['duration']):.3f} s")
    if a:
        print(f"audio     {a['sample_rate']} Hz, {a['channels']} ch")
    print(f"motion    median {med:.2f}, max {motion.max():.2f} at frame {int(motion.argmax())} "
          f"({motion.argmax() / fps:.2f} s)")
    print(f"cuts      {len(cuts)}" + (": " + ", ".join(f'{c / fps:.2f}s' for c in cuts) if cuts else ""))
    print(f"banner    visible (area >= 3%) in {int((area >= 0.03).sum())}/{len(f)} frames; "
          f"area {area.min():.3f}-{area.max():.3f}; top edge {np.nanmin(top):.3f}-{np.nanmax(top):.3f} of height")
    snd = None
    if a:
        rate = int(a['sample_rate']); x = audio(path, rate); hop = rate // 2
        snd = [20 * np.log10(np.sqrt(np.mean(x[i:i + hop] ** 2)) + 1e-9) for i in range(0, len(x) - hop + 1, hop)]
        h10 = rate // 10
        fine = np.array([20 * np.log10(np.sqrt(np.mean(x[i:i + h10] ** 2)) + 1e-9)
                         for i in range(0, len(x) - h10 + 1, h10)])
        rise = [(np.median(fine[k:k + 5]) - np.median(fine[k - 5:k]), k / 10) for k in range(5, len(fine) - 4)]
        db, t = max(rise)
        print(f"sound     biggest step up: {db:+.1f} dB at {t:.1f} s (median of 0.5 s after vs before)")
    print("\n  second | banner area | banner top | motion | sound dBFS (two halves)")
    for s in range(int(np.ceil(len(f) / fps))):

        if sl.start >= len(f):

        snd_txt = ""
        if snd:
            pair = snd[2 * s:2 * s + 2]
            snd_txt = " / ".join(f"{d:6.1f}" for d in pair)
        print(f"  {s:>2}-{s + 1:<3} |    {area[sl].mean():.3f}    |   {np.nanmean(top[sl]):.3f}    | {motion[sl].mean():6.2f} | {snd_txt}")
    if csv:

            fh.write("frame,t,banner_area,banner_top,motion\n")
            for i in range(len(f)):
                fh.write(f"{i},{i / fps:.4f},{area[i]:.4f},{top[i]:.4f},{motion[i]:.3f}\n")
        print(f"\nwrote {csv}")

title: Detect 5-Axis Rotary Reversals Before They Become Surface Marks
summary:
A collision check answers an important question: does the modeled tool assembly intersect the modeled part, fixture or machine envelope? It does not answer a different question: will the cutting contact remain stable while the rotary axes change direction?

A short surface witness line can appear near an A- or C-axis reversal even when simulation reports no collision. Possible contributors include a collapsing tool-tip feed, contact moving toward the center of a ball nose, an abrupt change in the inverse-kinematic solution, or a single damaged flute becoming visible as motion slows.

The useful diagnostic step is to align four things on one timeline:

  1. toolpath time,
  2. linear and rotary axis motion,
  3. contact-point or tool-vector data,
  4. the measured location of the mark on the part.

This post builds a deliberately small Python screen for recorded axis samples. It does not edit a toolpath or approve machine motion.

A narrow rotary-reversal screen

Suppose a controller or offline trace has been exported to CSV with time, linear position and rotary position. The following function marks a sample only when a rotary velocity changes sign and the calculated linear speed is below a review threshold.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from math import dist


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Sample:
    t: float
    xyz: tuple[float, float, float]
    a: float
    c: float


def delta(value, previous, dt):
    if dt <= 0:
        raise ValueError("timestamps must increase")
    return (value - previous) / dt


def changed_sign(previous, current, epsilon=1e-6):
    if abs(previous) <= epsilon or abs(current) <= epsilon:
        return False
    return (previous < 0 < current) or (current < 0 < previous)


def reversal_candidates(samples, low_linear_speed):
    if low_linear_speed <= 0:
        raise ValueError("low_linear_speed must be positive")
    if len(samples) < 3:
        return []

    segments = []
    for left, right in zip(samples, samples[1:]):
        dt = right.t - left.t
        segments.append({
            "end_time": right.t,
            "linear_speed": dist(left.xyz, right.xyz) / dt,
            "a_velocity": delta(right.a, left.a, dt),
            "c_velocity": delta(right.c, left.c, dt),
        })

    findings = []
    for previous, current in zip(segments, segments[1:]):
        axes = [
            axis
            for axis, key in (("A", "a_velocity"), ("C", "c_velocity"))
            if changed_sign(previous[key], current[key])
        ]
        if axes and current["linear_speed"] < low_linear_speed:
            findings.append({
                "time": current["end_time"],
                "axes": axes,
                "linear_speed": current["linear_speed"],
                "previous": previous,
                "current": current,
            })
    return findings

The result is named reversal_candidates, not bad_surface_points. A flagged timestamp is where an engineer should compare contact geometry, axis limits, controller interpolation and the actual surface. An unflagged timestamp is not proof of a good part.

Test a synthetic trace 

trace = [
    Sample(0.0, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), a=10.0, c=30.0),
    Sample(0.1, (1.0, 0.0, 0.0), a=10.5, c=30.3),
    Sample(0.2, (1.1, 0.0, 0.0), a=10.2, c=30.6),
    Sample(0.3, (2.1, 0.0, 0.0), a=9.9, c=30.9),
]

events = reversal_candidates(trace, low_linear_speed=2.0)
assert len(events) == 1
assert events[0]["axes"] == ["A"]
assert events[0]["time"] == 0.2

# A reversal at normal linear speed is intentionally not flagged by this screen.
fast_trace = [
    Sample(0.0, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), a=0.0, c=0.0),
    Sample(0.1, (1.0, 0.0, 0.0), a=1.0, c=0.0),
    Sample(0.2, (2.0, 0.0, 0.0), a=0.5, c=0.0),
]
assert reversal_candidates(fast_trace, low_linear_speed=2.0) == []

This example uses simple finite differences. A real trace may require angle unwrapping around 360 degrees, filtering that preserves short events, controller-specific units and synchronized tool-center-point data. Those requirements should be explicit rather than hidden inside a convenient plot.

What to inspect at each candidate

title: Python Lists: Why sort() and sorted() Affect Your Data Differently
summary:
Python Lists: Why sort() and sorted() Affect Your Data Differently

Sorting a list seems straightforward—until another variable unexpectedly changes, or your sorted result turns out to be None.

Understanding the difference between .sort() and sorted() becomes easier once you connect them to list references and copying.

Let’s explore that connection with a leaderboard.

1. Sorting through one name affects every alias 

scores = [75, 90, 60]
original_scores = scores

scores.sort()

print(scores)
print(original_scores)

Output:

[60, 75, 90]
[60, 75, 90]

The assignment original_scores = scores does not preserve the original order. Both names refer to the same list.

The .sort() method changes that list in place, so both names show its new order.

2. Why does assigning .sort() produce None?

Consider this small change:

scores = [75, 90, 60]
ordered_scores = scores.sort()

print(scores)
print(ordered_scores)

Output:

[60, 75, 90]
None

The list was sorted successfully.

However, .sort() returns None. Assigning its return value does not give you the sorted list.

Use it as a separate statement when you intend to modify the existing list:

scores.sort()

3. Use sorted() to create a new outer list

If you need to preserve the original order, use sorted():

scores = [75, 90, 60]
ordered_scores = sorted(scores)

print(scores)
print(ordered_scores)
print(scores is ordered_scores)

Output:

[75, 90, 60]
[60, 75, 90]
False

The original list stays unchanged, and ordered_scores refers to a new list.

Here is the key distinction:

Operation Changes the input list? Return value
scores.sort() Yes, potentially changing its order None
sorted(scores) No A new sorted list

4. A new sorted list can still share its elements

Now let’s store player names and scores in dictionaries:

players = [
    {"name": "Asha", "score": 75},
    {"name": "Ben", "score": 90},
]

leaderboard = sorted(
    players,
    key=lambda player: player["score"],
    reverse=True,
)

print([player["name"] for player in players])
print([player["name"] for player in leaderboard])

Output:

['Asha', 'Ben']
['Ben', 'Asha']

The key function tells Python to sort by each player’s score. reverse=True puts the highest score first.

The outer lists have different orders, but their elements are still the same dictionaries:

print(leaderboard[0] is players[1])

Output:

True

Changing Ben’s score through the leaderboard therefore changes the original data too:

leaderboard[0]["score"] = 95

print(players[1]["score"])

Output:

95

sorted() creates a new list; it does not recursively copy the objects inside it.

5. Create an independent leaderboard when needed

For this data structure, deep copying before sorting separates the player dictionaries:

from copy import deepcopy

players = [
    {"name": "Asha", "score": 75},
    {"name": "Ben", "score": 90},
]

leaderboard = sorted(
    deepcopy(players),
    key=lambda player: player["score"],
    reverse=True,
)

leaderboard[0]["score"] = 95

print(players[1]["score"])
print(leaderboard[0]["score"])

Output:

90
95

Whether you need that independence depends on your goal.

If the leaderboard should display the same player records in another order, sharing them may be appropriate. If it should be a separate snapshot, copying the nested data may be necessary.

Separate ordering from copying

When sorting Python data, ask two questions:

  • Should the original list’s order change?
  • Should the elements themselves remain shared?

.sort() and sorted() address the ordering decision. Copying determines which mutable objects can change independently.

For further reading, see the official Python Sorting HOWTO.

title: Why Does My Python Function Remember Previous Calls?
summary:
Why Does My Python Function Remember Previous Calls?

You call a function twice, expecting each call to start with an empty list. Instead, the second result contains data from the first call.

The cause may be a mutable default argument: a list created when the function is defined and reused across calls.

Let’s see how this connects to references and copying.

1. The list that keeps growing

Consider a function that records completed lessons:

def complete_lesson(lesson, completed=[]):
    completed.append(lesson)
    return completed

print(complete_lesson("Variables"))
print(complete_lesson("Loops"))

Output:

['Variables']
['Variables', 'Loops']

Why does the second call include "Variables"?

Python evaluates default argument expressions when it executes the function definition. It does not create a new default list each time you call the function.

Both calls use and modify the same list.

2. Returned results can share that list too

The sharing becomes clearer when we keep both results:

def complete_lesson(lesson, completed=[]):
    completed.append(lesson)
    return completed

first = complete_lesson("Variables")
second = complete_lesson("Loops")

print(first)
print(second)
print(first is second)

Output:

['Variables', 'Loops']
['Variables', 'Loops']
True

The function returns its list without copying it.

Consequently, first and second refer to the same object. The second call changes what you see through first too.

3. Create a fresh list inside the function

If each call should start independently, use None as the default:

def complete_lesson(lesson, completed=None):
    if completed is None:
        completed = []

    completed.append(lesson)
    return completed

first = complete_lesson("Variables")
second = complete_lesson("Loops")

print(first)
print(second)
print(first is second)

Output:

['Variables']
['Loops']
False

The list expression [] now runs inside the function whenever the argument is omitted or explicitly set to None.

Each of these calls creates a separate list.

4. An explicitly supplied list can still change

The None pattern prevents accidental sharing of a default list. It does not prevent the function from modifying a list supplied by the caller.

def complete_lesson(lesson, completed=None):
    if completed is None:
        completed = []

    completed.append(lesson)
    return completed

my_lessons = ["Variables"]
result = complete_lesson("Loops", my_lessons)

print(my_lessons)
print(result is my_lessons)

Output:

['Variables', 'Loops']
True

The parameter completed refers to the caller’s list. Calling .append() modifies that object.

This behaviour can be useful, but it should be intentional.

5. Copy the input when you want a new result

If the function should preserve the supplied list, copy it before making changes:

def complete_lesson(lesson, completed=None):
    if completed is None:
        updated = []
    else:
        updated = completed.copy()

    updated.append(lesson)
    return updated

my_lessons = ["Variables"]
result = complete_lesson("Loops", my_lessons)

print(my_lessons)
print(result)
print(result is my_lessons)

Output:

['Variables']
['Variables', 'Loops']
False

For this list of strings, a shallow copy provides the separation we need.

For nested mutable data, you would also need to consider whether the inner objects should remain shared.

Three questions to ask when reading a function

When a function accepts or returns a list, check:

  1. When is the list created?
  2. Does the function modify an existing list?
  3. Does the returned value share an object with another variable?

These questions help explain both mutable default arguments and unexpected changes to function inputs.

For further reading, see the official Python tutorial on default argument values.

title: Whisper transcription and SRT subtitles with the OpenAI SDK, without an OpenAI account (one-line change)
summary:
The OpenAI SDK is a good HTTP client for audio. client.audio.transcriptions.create() handles multipart uploads,
response_format="srt" gives you subtitles, and client.audio.speech.create() streams MP3. Plenty of tools,
scripts and agents are already written against it.

The SDK doesn't care whose server it talks to. Point base_url at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint and the same code
runs. That matters when:

  • the person running your script has no OpenAI account or card on file;
  • you want an hour of audio to cost less than OpenAI's $0.36 (whisper-1 at $0.006 a minute);
  • you are an agent that can pay per request but cannot sign up for anything.

The one-line change 

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://agent-data-tools.revmesh2074.workers.dev/v1",  # <- the only change
)

with open("meeting.mp3", "rb") as f:
    srt = client.audio.transcriptions.create(model="whisper-1", file=f, response_format="srt")
open("meeting.srt", "w").write(srt)

client.audio.speech.create(model="tts-1", voice="alloy", input="Your order has shipped.").write_to_file("hi.mp3")

The Node SDK takes baseURL in the same way. json, text, srt, vtt and verbose_json all come back in
OpenAI's format, and OpenAI voice names map to similar voices. We ran each of these calls with the stock
openai packages (Python and Node) before writing this.

What is behind it

Disclosure: the endpoint is ours (SpellzCode). It runs Whisper large-v3-turbo for transcription and Deepgram Aura
voices for speech. The trade-offs, honestly:

OpenAI This endpoint
Account to start Yes, plus a card No: a $1 card top-up gives a key, or an agent pays per call in USDC (x402)
One hour of audio $0.36 (whisper-1), $0.18 (gpt-4o-mini-transcribe) $0.05 per file up to 60 min (/transcribe/long)
Short clip per minute $0.01 per file up to 5 MB
Subtitles srt / vtt srt / vtt
Speech languages many English and Spanish
Failed calls never charged

If you need many speech languages or a specific OpenAI model such as gpt-4o-transcribe, stay on OpenAI. If you mostly
transcribe and want no account and a lower bill, this is a one-line switch.

Long recordings

The OpenAI endpoint caps uploads at 25 MB. For meetings and podcasts there is a separate call that takes up to 60
minutes of MP3 or WAV, splits it into parts and joins the timestamps:

curl -s -G "https://agent-data-tools.revmesh2074.workers.dev/transcribe/long" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" \
  --data-urlencode "url=https://example.com/episode.mp3" \
  --data-urlencode "subtitles=srt" | jq -r .subtitles > episode.srt

A 9.7-minute speech came back in 3 parts with continuous SRT timestamps.

Code ElevenLabs users can keep

The same endpoint also answers POST /v1/speech-to-text and POST /v1/text-to-speech/{voice_id} in ElevenLabs'
shape, with the same xi-api-key header. Only the host changes.

title: When a Python List Copy Is Only Half a Copy
summary:
When a Python List Copy Is Only Half a Copy

You used .copy(), but changing your copied data still affected the original.

Did the copy fail?

The answer depends on what is inside your list. A shallow copy creates a new outer list, while its elements still refer to the same objects.

Let’s explore this through a weekly schedule.

1. Adding a day keeps the original unchanged 

schedule = [
    ["Monday", "Python"],
    ["Tuesday", "SQL"],
]

revised = schedule.copy()
revised.append(["Wednesday", "Git"])

print(len(schedule))
print(len(revised))

Output:

2
3

Calling .copy() created a separate outer list.

Appending a new entry changes only revised. So far, the copy behaves exactly as you might expect.

2. Editing an existing day affects both lists

Now start again and update Monday’s subject:

schedule = [
    ["Monday", "Python"],
    ["Tuesday", "SQL"],
]

revised = schedule.copy()
revised[0][1] = "JavaScript"

print(schedule[0])
print(revised[0])

Output:

['Monday', 'JavaScript']
['Monday', 'JavaScript']

The outer lists are separate, but their first elements refer to the same inner list.

This expression:

revised[0][1] = "JavaScript"

accesses that shared inner list and replaces one of its elements.

You can inspect the relationship directly:

print(schedule is revised)
print(schedule[0] is revised[0])

Output:

False
True

3. Replacing a whole entry behaves differently

Compare the previous example with this one:

schedule = [
    ["Monday", "Python"],
    ["Tuesday", "SQL"],
]

revised = schedule.copy()
revised[0] = ["Monday", "JavaScript"]

print(schedule[0])
print(revised[0])

Output:

['Monday', 'Python']
['Monday', 'JavaScript']

Here, we create a new inner list and place it into the separate outer list revised.

The original Monday entry remains unchanged.

The difference is the level at which the assignment happens:

Statement What changes?
revised[0][1] = "JavaScript" An element inside the shared inner list
revised[0] = ["Monday", "JavaScript"] An element inside the separate outer list

4. Copying each row can provide enough independence

For this schedule, we can copy both the outer list and each row:

schedule = [
    ["Monday", "Python"],
    ["Tuesday", "SQL"],
]

revised = [row.copy() for row in schedule]
revised[0][1] = "JavaScript"

print(schedule[0])
print(revised[0])

Output:

['Monday', 'Python']
['Monday', 'JavaScript']

The list comprehension builds a new outer list. Each row.copy() also creates a new row.

This works for our schedule because each row contains strings. It does not recursively copy every possible level of nested data.

5. Another nesting level introduces sharing again

Suppose each day contains a list of subjects:

schedule = [
    ["Monday", ["Python", "SQL"]],
    ["Tuesday", ["Git"]],
]

revised = [row.copy() for row in schedule]
revised[0][1].append("Testing")

print(schedule[0][1])
print(revised[0][1])

Output:

['Python', 'SQL', 'Testing']
['Python', 'SQL', 'Testing']

We copied the outer list and each row, but the subject lists inside those rows remain shared.

When this nested data needs to be independent, use deepcopy():

from copy import deepcopy

schedule = [
    ["Monday", ["Python", "SQL"]],
    ["Tuesday", ["Git"]],
]

revised = deepcopy(schedule)
revised[0][1].append("Testing")

print(schedule[0][1])
print(revised[0][1])

Output:

['Python', 'SQL']
['Python', 'SQL', 'Testing']

For this structure, the nested subject lists are now independent.

Choose the copy that matches your change

Before copying a list, consider what you intend to modify.

  • Adding or removing outer entries: a shallow copy may be enough.
  • Editing individual rows: copying each row may be enough for simple data.
  • Changing mutable objects deeper inside the structure: consider a deep copy.

The useful question is: Which objects will my next operation modify, and are those objects still shared?

For further reading, see the official Python documentation on shallow and deep copying.

title: A prompt-injected model cannot skip your approval step
summary:
A human-in-the-loop design usually has the same shape: the model proposes an action, the graph stops at an approval step, a person says yes or no, and only then does the tool run. The guarantee you want is that the model has no way to reach the tool without passing the stop.

That guarantee holds only if every path around the stop is closed, including the paths a model can influence by text alone. A model that has read a hostile web page or a poisoned document can be steered into producing unusual output: a tool name you did not expect, a routing hint, a message that looks like a human answer. This post lists the places where 10xGraph decides on the graph's side instead of trusting that output, and what you still have to do yourself. It describes behaviour and design, not ways to attack a particular app.

10xGraph is open-source, self-hosted infrastructure for AI applications. You write the agents, tools and tasks; 10xGraph runs them behind an API server with authentication, role-based access, tenant isolation, durable state in Postgres and Redis, background jobs, metrics and tracing, and generates Docker and Kubernetes deploy files. MIT licensed, by 10xScale. Formerly Agentflow.

The reference pages are Interrupts and the security model.

Handoffs only go where a handoff tool says

Handoff is how one agent passes the conversation to another, through a tool made with create_handoff_tool. If any tool call named transfer_to_ moved the run to node , a steered model could name a node that your edges never lead to, and that includes a node behind an approval step.

So a handoff is honoured only when the ToolNode holds a tool of that name created by create_handoff_tool. Any other transfer_to_* call is an ordinary tool call, and if no such tool exists it gets the usual "Tool not found" result.

The same rule covers Command(goto=...) returned from your own code. A target that is neither a node in the graph nor END raises GraphError with code GRAPH_007, naming the node it came from and the unknown target.

Starting a run at a chosen node with current_node is a separate, intended feature (a frontend can send the agent the user picked). If a node needs an entry guard, enforce it inside the graph. The change above is about what the model can do, not what your caller can do.

Tools hidden by tools_tags cannot be called

An Agent can advertise only the tools that match tools_tags. Showing the model only the tagged tools is not enough on its own, because the ToolNode could still run any registered name the model happened to guess.

So the Agent records the names it advertised on the assistant message (metadata["allowed_tools"]), and the dispatch step refuses a call to anything outside that list with the same "Tool not found" error. If you use tags to keep a destructive tool away from a low-trust agent, the tag holds at run time and not just in the prompt.

A tool name cannot be claimed twice

When a ToolNode also connects to an MCP server, a remote tool could otherwise take over the name of a local tool, so calls meant for your function would go to the server. A collision between an MCP tool and a local or remote tool on the same ToolNode raises ValueError ("Rename one of them"), and the check runs outside the code that swallows connection errors, so it cannot be hidden by a failed server ping.

Forged tool results are refused

Remote tools run on the client, and the client sends the result back to resume the run. That is the one case where the API accepts a message with the tool role, and it is narrow.

  • Client messages may only have the user role. The assistant and system roles are refused, and so is a tool message that carries anything other than tool results.
  • A tool result is accepted only for a remote tool call that is waiting for one on that thread. A result for a call the model never made, a second result for the same call, or a result for a server tool is refused.
  • A client tool can never carry the name of a server tool. Otherwise a client could declare a tool with the name of the one paused for approval and post a "result" for it.

The effect is that the approval path cannot be satisfied by pretending to be the model or the tool.

A resume answers one specific question

A resume carries a value, and the value can be bound to the prompt it answers:

  • The client can send interrupt_id with the resume on invoke, stream and WebSocket. If the thread is not paused, or is paused at another interrupt (a stale tab, a retried request after the first answer was consumed), the API answers 409 and records nothing. This is how a late "yes" fails to approve a different request.
  • The core checks the id again and, when the interrupt declared a response_schema (a JSON Schema), validates the value against it. A mismatch raises InterruptMismatchError (INTERRUPT_001), and a value that does not satisfy the schema raises ResumeValidationError (INTERRUPT_002). Nothing is recorded in either case.

The API checks the id first and answers 409 before a stream starts. It also passes the id to the core, which enforces it again.

from tenxgraph.utils import interrupt

async def refund(amount: float) -> str:
    decision = interrupt(
        {"amount": amount},
        message=f"Refund ${amount}?",
        reason="tool_approval",
        response_schema={
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"approved": {"type": "boolean"}},
            "required": ["approved"],
        },
    )
    if not decision or not decision.get("approved"):
        return "Refund declined"
    return issue_refund(amount)

Without interrupt_id, a resume answers whatever the thread is paused at, as before. Send the id from any client where a person can have two tabs open.

What you still own

  • None of this makes a model trustworthy. It removes shortcuts around your graph.
  • Authentication, role-based access and ownership are separate layers, covered in the security model. Another user's thread answers 404. Permissions apply per route; there are no per-tool permissions, so decide inside the tool who may do what.
  • A tool that must be safe against a steered model should still validate its own arguments and use idempotency keys. See Interrupts for how to place the stop before the tool, not after it.

Frequently asked questions

Does this stop prompt injection?

No. Nothing stops a model from being steered by text it reads. These controls limit what a steered model can do to the parts of the graph you did not give it: the route it takes, the tools it can call and the approval a human gives.

Can a client approve an interrupt by sending a tool result?

No. The API accepts a tool result only as the answer to a remote tool call that is waiting for one. A result for a server tool, for a call the model never made, or a second result for the same call is refused.

What does interrupt_id add to a resume?

It ties the answer to the exact prompt the human saw. If the thread is paused at a different interrupt, or not paused at all, the API answers 409 and nothing is recorded.

title: Python List Copies: Why Small Changes Can Have Unexpected Results
summary:
Python List Copies: Why Small Changes Can Have Unexpected Results

Imagine copying a player’s inventory before updating it. You add a new item to the copy, then discover that the original inventory has changed too.

Python is behaving consistently—but understanding that behaviour requires knowing which objects your variables refer to.

Let’s explore list references and copying through a different set of examples.

1. Two names can share one inventory 

player_items = ["torch", "map"]
saved_items = player_items

player_items.remove("torch")

print(player_items)
print(saved_items)

Output:

['map']
['map']

The assignment saved_items = player_items gives the existing list another name. It does not save an independent snapshot.

Both names refer to the same list, so removing an item through player_items also affects what you see through saved_items.

Create a separate outer list when you need a snapshot:

player_items = ["torch", "map"]
saved_items = player_items.copy()

player_items.remove("torch")

print(player_items)
print(saved_items)

Output:

['map']
['torch', 'map']

For this list of strings, a shallow copy provides the separation we need.

2. += and + can behave differently

These two operations look similar, but their effect on a list’s aliases differs.

Using += 

tasks = ["read"]
shared_tasks = tasks

tasks += ["practise"]

print(tasks)
print(shared_tasks)

Output:

['read', 'practise']
['read', 'practise']

For a built-in list, += extends the existing list. Since shared_tasks refers to that list too, it sees the change.

Using + 

tasks = ["read"]
shared_tasks = tasks

tasks = tasks + ["practise"]

print(tasks)
print(shared_tasks)

Output:

['read', 'practise']
['read']

Here, + creates a new list. The assignment then makes tasks refer to it.

shared_tasks still refers to the original list.

Remember: For built-in lists, += modifies the existing object, while + produces a new one.

3. A function can modify the caller’s list

Consider a function that adds a participant:

def register(names):
    names.append("Maya")

participants = ["Arun", "Leah"]
register(participants)

print(participants)

Output:

['Arun', 'Leah', 'Maya']

During the call, the parameter names refers to the same list as participants. The function modifies that shared list.

However, reassigning the parameter behaves differently:

def register(names):
    names = names + ["Maya"]
    return names

participants = ["Arun", "Leah"]
updated = register(participants)

print(participants)
print(updated)

Output:

['Arun', 'Leah']
['Arun', 'Leah', 'Maya']

The expression names + ["Maya"] creates a new list. Reassigning the local name names does not reassign participants.

The function returns the new list so the caller can use it.

4. Equal lists are not necessarily the same list

Python provides two comparisons that answer different questions:

first = [4, 8]
second = first.copy()
third = first

print(first == second)
print(first is second)
print(first is third)

Output:

True
False
True

Here is what each comparison checks:

Expression Question
first == second Do these lists contain equal values?
first is second Are these references to the same object?
first is third Are these references to the same object?

Use == to compare list contents. Use is when you specifically need to check object identity.

5. A copied list can still share dictionaries

Nested data does not have to contain inner lists. The same issue arises with dictionaries inside a list.

products = [
    {"name": "Notebook", "stock": 12},
    {"name": "Pen", "stock": 30},
]

snapshot = products.copy()
snapshot[0]["stock"] = 0

print(products[0]["stock"])
print(snapshot[0]["stock"])

Output:

0
0

The outer list was copied, but the dictionaries inside it remain shared.

For this data, a deep copy creates independent dictionaries too:

from copy import deepcopy

products = [
    {"name": "Notebook", "stock": 12},
    {"name": "Pen", "stock": 30},
]

snapshot = deepcopy(products)
snapshot[0]["stock"] = 0

print(products[0]["stock"])
print(snapshot[0]["stock"])

Output:

12
0

Choose the copy depth based on which mutable objects need to be independent. Deep copying can do unnecessary work when sharing nested objects is intentional.

How to reason through these examples

Before predicting the output, identify:

  1. Which lines create new lists.
  2. Which names refer to the same list.
  3. Which operations modify existing objects.
  4. Whether a copy still contains shared mutable objects.

This approach helps you explain the behaviour instead of memorising individual examples.

For more detail, see the official Python documentation on shallow and deep copying.

Python is behaving consistently—but understanding that behaviour requires knowing which objects your variables refer to.

Let’s explore list references and copying through a different set of examples.

1. Two names can share one inventory 

player_items = ["torch", "map"]
saved_items = player_items

player_items.remove("torch")

print(player_items)
print(saved_items)

Output:

['map']
['map']

The assignment saved_items = player_items gives the existing list another name. It does not save an independent snapshot.

Both names refer to the same list, so removing an item through player_items also affects what you see through saved_items.

Create a separate outer list when you need a snapshot:

player_items = ["torch", "map"]
saved_items = player_items.copy()

player_items.remove("torch")

print(player_items)
print(saved_items)

Output:

['map']
['torch', 'map']

For this list of strings, a shallow copy provides the separation we need.

2. += and + can behave differently

These two operations look similar, but their effect on a list’s aliases differs.

Using += 

tasks = ["read"]
shared_tasks = tasks

tasks += ["practise"]

print(tasks)
print(shared_tasks)

Output:

['read', 'practise']
['read', 'practise']

For a built-in list, += extends the existing list. Since shared_tasks refers to that list too, it sees the change.

Using + 

tasks = ["read"]
shared_tasks = tasks

tasks = tasks + ["practise"]

print(tasks)
print(shared_tasks)

Output:

['read', 'practise']
['read']

Here, + creates a new list. The assignment then makes tasks refer to it.

shared_tasks still refers to the original list.

Remember: For built-in lists, += modifies the existing object, while + produces a new one.

3. A function can modify the caller’s list

Consider a function that adds a participant:

def register(names):
    names.append("Maya")

participants = ["Arun", "Leah"]
register(participants)

print(participants)

Output:

['Arun', 'Leah', 'Maya']

During the call, the parameter names refers to the same list as participants. The function modifies that shared list.

However, reassigning the parameter behaves differently:

def register(names):
    names = names + ["Maya"]
    return names

participants = ["Arun", "Leah"]
updated = register(participants)

print(participants)
print(updated)

Output:

['Arun', 'Leah']
['Arun', 'Leah', 'Maya']

The expression names + ["Maya"] creates a new list. Reassigning the local name names does not reassign participants.

The function returns the new list so the caller can use it.

4. Equal lists are not necessarily the same list

Python provides two comparisons that answer different questions:

first = [4, 8]
second = first.copy()
third = first

print(first == second)
print(first is second)
print(first is third)

Output:

True
False
True

Here is what each comparison checks:

Expression Question
first == second Do these lists contain equal values?
first is second Are these references to the same object?
first is third Are these references to the same object?

Use == to compare list contents. Use is when you specifically need to check object identity.

5. A copied list can still share dictionaries

Nested data does not have to contain inner lists. The same issue arises with dictionaries inside a list.

products = [
    {"name": "Notebook", "stock": 12},
    {"name": "Pen", "stock": 30},
]

snapshot = products.copy()
snapshot[0]["stock"] = 0

print(products[0]["stock"])
print(snapshot[0]["stock"])

Output:

0
0

The outer list was copied, but the dictionaries inside it remain shared.

For this data, a deep copy creates independent dictionaries too:

products = [
    {"name": "Notebook", "stock": 12},
    {"name": "Pen", "stock": 30},
]

snapshot = deepcopy(products)
snapshot[0]["stock"] = 0

print(products[0]["stock"])
print(snapshot[0]["stock"])

Output:

12
0

Choose the copy depth based on which mutable objects need to be independent. Deep copying can do unnecessary work when sharing nested objects is intentional.

How to reason through these examples

Before predicting the output, identify:

  1. Which lines create new lists.
  2. Which names refer to the same list.
  3. Which operations modify existing objects.
  4. Whether a copy still contains shared mutable objects.

This approach helps you explain the behaviour instead of memorising individual examples.

title: Empresia Scraper in Python: Company Reports and Daily New Incorporations from the BORME
summary:
Empresia.es is a free Spanish company directory built on the Commercial Registry. Every company has a report with its CIF, CNAE activity code, share capital, sales band, employees, address, phones, board, officers and the announcements it published in the BORME (Spain's Official Gazette of the Commercial Registry). It also lists, day by day and province by province, every company that was incorporated, dissolved or changed its capital. For lead generation, KYC or market research, that is a clean B2B dataset. Here is how to pull it into Python, and what to watch out for.

Why not plain requests 

import requests

r = requests.get("https://www.empresia.es/empresa/mercadona/")
print(r.status_code)  # 200, for now

Empresia renders everything on the server, so a single request works. The problem starts at volume: the site sits behind Cloudflare, and a crawl of thousands of company pages from one IP is exactly what gets throttled. Sending each request through Scrape.do rotates the IP on every call and retries failures. A plain request is enough, no extra parameters: 1 credit per page, about 2 seconds.

TOKEN = ""

def fetch(url):
    r = requests.get("https://api.scrape.do/", params={"token": TOKEN, "url": url}, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.text

Where the data is on a company page

There is no JSON-LD and no API behind the page. The data sits in a few predictable blocks:

  1. div.datos-ident: name, phones, fax, address, websites and e-mail, then label/value pairs (span.list-group-item-heading followed by p.list-group-item-text) for CIF, incorporation date, share capital, sales band, registry, last filed accounts, employees, governing body and auditor.
  2. #organigrama: the board, one li per person with the role after the link.
  3. #ListaRelaciones: officers with appointment and removal dates.
  4. #ListaEventos: the BORME timeline (changes of address, appointments, capital increases), each with a link to the official PDF.

Two details catch people out. The e-mail is not in the HTML as text: Cloudflare replaces it with [email protected] and a data-cfemail attribute, a hex string whose first byte is the XOR key for the rest. And the sales figure is a band ("Superior a 2.500.000 euros"), kept in the title of a tooltip, not in the visible text.

from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

def decode_cfemail(hex_str):
    data = bytes.fromhex(hex_str)
    return bytes(b ^ data[0] for b in data[1:]).decode()


def company(slug):
    soup = BeautifulSoup(fetch(f"https://www.empresia.es/empresa/{slug}/"), "html.parser")
    box = soup.select_one("div.datos-ident")
    fields = {}
    for label in box.select("span.list-group-item-heading"):
        value = label.find_next_sibling("p", class_="list-group-item-text")
        if value:
            fields[label.get_text(strip=True)] = value
    purpose, _, cnae = fields["Objeto social"].get_text("\n", strip=True).partition("\nCNAE ")
    sales = fields["Ventas"].select_one("[title]")
    email = box.select_one("[data-cfemail]")
    return {
        "name": box.select_one("span.bolder").get_text(strip=True),
        "cif": fields["CIF"].get_text(strip=True),
        "cnae": cnae,
        "purpose": purpose,
        "capital": fields["Capital social"].get_text(strip=True),
        "sales_band": sales["title"] if sales else "",
        "employees": fields["Número empleados"].get_text(strip=True),
        "registry": fields["Registro"].get_text(strip=True),
        "email": decode_cfemail(email["data-cfemail"]) if email else "",
        "board": [(a.get_text(strip=True), a.find_next_sibling(string=True).strip())
                  for a in soup.select("#organigrama li a")],
    }

In a live run on Mercadona this returned the CIF, CNAE 4711, the sales band, 108,742 employees, the registry (Valencia), the decoded e-mail and 13 board members, from one request. Values Empresia shows as - (Mercadona's share capital, for example) come back as -, so clean them before loading the data anywhere.

Every new company, every day

The most useful part of Empresia for lead generation is the BORME by day. Each weekday the gazette publishes every incorporation, and Empresia lists them by act and province:

/borme/fecha/2026-11-13/acto/constitucion/provincia/barcelona/

Change constitucion to disolucion, ampliacion-de-capital, cambio-de-domicilio-social or nombramientos for other acts. On 13 November 2026 there were 41 act types across 34 provinces, and Barcelona alone had 71 new companies. Each row links to the announcement, which has a small table with the registry, start date, share capital, corporate purpose and registered address:

import csv

BASE = "https://www.empresia.es"


def new_companies(date, province):
    url = f"{BASE}/borme/fecha/{date}/acto/constitucion/provincia/{province}/"
    soup = BeautifulSoup(fetch(url), "html.parser")
    for row in soup.select("#contenido table tbody tr"):
        name = row.select_one("a.lk")
        event = row.select_one('a[href*="/evento/"]')
        yield name.get_text(strip=True), BASE + event["href"]


def announcement(url):
    soup = BeautifulSoup(fetch(url), "html.parser")
    cells = [td.get_text(" ", strip=True) for td in soup.select("div.eventonly table td")]
    return dict(zip(cells[::2], cells[1::2]))


with open("new_companies.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["company", "registry", "start", "capital", "purpose", "address"])
    for name, link in new_companies("2026-11-13", "barcelona"):
        d = announcement(link)
        writer.writerow([name, d.get("Registro"), d.get("Fecha inicio"), d.get("Capital"),
                         d.get("Objeto social"), d.get("Domicilio")])

That is one request for the list plus one per company: 72 credits for a full day of Barcelona incorporations. Run it on a schedule and you have a daily feed of companies that did not exist last week.

Search, and its ceiling

Search is /busqueda/?q=&pagina=. Results mix companies (EMPRESA), officers (DIRECTIVO) and trademarks (DISTINTIVO), and Empresia stops at 100 results: past the last page it quietly sends page 1 again, so compare the "Mostrando del X al Y" counter before trusting a page. For anything broader than a name, the BORME lists by province are the better entry point.

Skip the code

The same scraper is an open-source package with a CLI:

pip install empresia-scraper
export SCRAPEDO_TOKEN=<your_token>
empresia-scraper telefonica mercadona -f csv -o companies.csv
empresia-scraper --borme 2026-11-13 --province madrid --details -o new_companies.json

Source and tests: github.com/bugrahansss/empresia-scraper

The data comes from public registers, but officers are real people and their names are personal data under the GDPR. Use it for legitimate purposes such as B2B research or KYC, keep only what you need, honour objection requests and respect Empresia's terms.
